name: Groove pancreatitis
aliases: cystic dystrophy of the duodenal wall

reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A form of focal chronic pancreatitis centred on the groove between the pancreatic head, the duodenum, and the common bile duct
Typically affects middle-aged men with a heavy alcohol history and is often associated with smoking
Presents with recurrent upper abdominal pain, postprandial vomiting, and weight loss, sometimes with jaundice from bile duct narrowing
Imaging shows sheet-like fibrous tissue in the groove, duodenal wall thickening, and small cysts within the duodenal wall or paraduodenal region
Duodenal luminal narrowing and reduced motility from wall oedema and fibrosis can produce a gastric outlet obstruction picture
The principal difficulty is distinguishing it from pancreatic head or periampullary carcinoma, which it can closely resemble

Management is initially conservative with alcohol and smoking cessation, pain control, and duodenal rest, reserving pancreaticoduodenectomy for intractable symptoms or when malignancy cannot be excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Groove pancreatitis is a segmental chronic pancreatitis affecting the anatomical groove bounded by the dorsocranial pancreatic head, the duodenal wall, and the common bile duct. Impaired outflow of pancreatic secretions through the minor papilla and the dorsal duct region, frequently in the setting of alcohol excess and smoking, is thought to provoke inflammation and dense fibrosis in this space, often with cystic change (cystic dystrophy) within the duodenal wall itself. The resulting scar tissue thickens and stiffens the duodenal wall, can narrow the duodenal lumen and distal bile duct, and produces a mass-like appearance that mimics a periampullary neoplasm.
additionalDifferentials: Cholangiocarcinoma involving the distal bile duct
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT to characterise groove soft tissue, duodenal wall thickening, and cysts
MRI with MRCP to assess the biliary and pancreatic ducts and detect intramural cysts
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle biopsy to sample the groove and exclude malignancy
Upper endoscopy to inspect the duodenal mucosa and assess luminal narrowing
Serum CA 19-9 to help weigh the likelihood of carcinoma
Liver function tests to detect biliary obstruction
redFlags: Features suggesting periampullary or pancreatic carcinoma, such as a discrete enhancing mass or vascular involvement
Marked or persistent weight loss with an unexplained mass
reference.prognosis: Symptoms often improve with abstinence from alcohol and smoking and supportive care, but disease may be relapsing; surgical resection is frequently effective for refractory pain or obstruction and, importantly, confirms the benign nature of the lesion when carcinoma has been a concern.
pitfalls: Mistaking the fibrotic groove mass for a resectable or unresectable pancreatic carcinoma
Over-reliance on a single biopsy, as sampling error can miss coexisting malignancy
Failing to address ongoing alcohol and tobacco use, which perpetuates the disease
Attributing all upper gastrointestinal symptoms to the pancreas while overlooking duodenal obstruction
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Adsay and Zamboni, paraduodenal pancreatitis reviews
Radiology reviews of groove pancreatitis imaging
management: Advise complete abstinence from alcohol and smoking cessation as the key modifiable drivers of the disease
Manage pain with analgesia and pancreatic rest, and provide nutritional support with pancreatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency
Relieve duodenal or gastric outlet obstruction and biliary narrowing, using endoscopic decompression or stenting where feasible
Exclude periampullary or pancreatic head carcinoma with endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy before committing to conservative treatment
Offer surgical resection such as pancreaticoduodenectomy for refractory pain, obstruction or persistent diagnostic uncertainty, which also confirms the benign nature of the lesion
Coordinate multidisciplinary hepatobiliary, pancreatology and surgical review

Red flag present (enhancing mass, progressive jaundice, weight loss, outlet obstruction)?
Urgent endoscopic ultrasound and biopsy for suspected carcinoma or jaundice
CT, MRCP, endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy, endoscopy and CA 19-9
Does EUS-guided biopsy exclude periampullary or pancreatic carcinoma?
Consider head or periampullary carcinoma, duodenal tumour or autoimmune pancreatitis
Complete alcohol abstinence and smoking cessation
Analgesia, pancreatic rest and enzyme replacement
Endoscopic decompression or stenting of obstruction where feasible
Surgical resection for refractory pain, obstruction or persistent uncertainty
